This document will go over the many, many ways data can be stored and how to read them into R. This will be a living document; growing as time goes on to explore topics more in depth, add new methods of reading in data, and add new data formats that can be read in.

# Text: Free-form

There is not too much advice I can give here that applies to every free-form text file because one is going to be different. 

There may be some standardization if a particular software is writing the files (e.g., modeling software writing standard outputs) in which case it would be best to write a custom function, or find one online if it exists, to parse that file.

Start with one of these functions below:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
readLines()

#or

readr::read_lines()
```
:::


I usually just use `readLines()` because it reduces the need for a dependency (the `{readr}` package), but `read_lines()` does have some additional functionality like the ability to skip a certain number of rows.

One example may be trying to parse information from a text file that is the output of some statistical software. Here, I've just run a quick ANOVA with some assumptions tests and written the output to a text file.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lines <- readLines("./data_storage_formats/mtcars_test_results.txt")

cat(lines,sep = "\n")
```

This also gets into the realm of listings and some loggers, depending on how they have been set up.

## Loggers

Some loggers output free-form text, but others could be fixed-width or even delimited. For the free-form versions, again, you are going to need a custom parser. I do find these easier than listings because they usually don't wrap records onto multiple lines as there is no width restrictions like listing have.




## Listings







Listings are a whole different discussion. I really do not understand how in the 21st century, the best way to communicate record level data is to print those records into a file. This causes several issues with wrapping labels and records over multiple lines because the document the listing is printed on has a limited number of characters wide it can be.
If pulling records from an XPT, labels are allowed to be 40 characters but the listing usually has to be about 80-120 characters wide depending on the text size of the document it is going in. That means variable labels often have to be wrapped, otherwise you could only end up with 2-3 columns before hitting your max number of characters. 
If there are too many variables, the listing is split and the next set of variables are printed with only a row number to link it to the other variables of the same record. 
It still blows my mind that this is still common practice instead of providing an actual data file (even and excel file would be better, and that is saying a lot coming from me). 

Unlike fixed-width, each column can be a different width so parsing these is a challenge usually requiring a custom function to determine the start and end of each column to then split off of and get into a data frame. If variables are wrapping, you will need to retain the row number and merge the chunks back together.

Only advice I can give without getting into the weeds too much is to read in the data using one of the functions below to get the text into R, then figure out any rules you can detect on the structure and spacing to parse out what you need.

# Domain specific

There are so many formats that are only used in specific domains and are less common. 

These could be things like signal/audio, DICOM, or types specifically for things like genomics.
